title: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
summary: How ColBERT keeps one vector per token and scores with MaxSim, how ColBERTv2 and PLAID make that small and fast, and how ColPali applies the same idea to images of document pages.
outcomes: Explain why late interaction sits between bi-encoders and cross-encoders in cost and quality
Compute a MaxSim score by hand from query and document token embeddings
Estimate per-document storage for multi-vector indexes and the savings from 1- and 2-bit residual compression
Trace PLAID's centroid interaction and pruning stages and explain why they are safe filters
Explain how ColPali scores page images patch by patch and when it beats OCR pipelines

lessons.title: Why one vector per document leaves accuracy behind

blocks.md:
Recall the two neural rankers you already know. A **bi-encoder** (the semantic search model) turns the query into one vector and each document into one vector, and scores with a dot product. Document vectors are computed offline, so a query costs one encoder pass plus a vector search.

A **cross-encoder** (the reranker) feeds the query and one document *together* through a transformer, so every query word can attend to every document word. It is far more accurate, but nothing can be precomputed: ranking $k$ documents means $k$ full transformer passes at query time.

The ColBERT paper (Khattab and Zaharia, SIGIR 2020) put numbers on that gap for MS MARCO passage ranking, re-ranking the BM25 top 1000 per query on one V100 GPU:

- BM25 alone: MRR@10 of 16.7 (MRR@10 averages 1/rank of the first relevant passage in the top 10 over queries, shown x100).
- BERT-base cross-encoder: MRR@10 of 34.7, but **10,700 ms** and about 97 trillion FLOPs per query.

A search system cannot spend ten seconds per query. The question ColBERT asks: can we keep most of the word-level matching of the cross-encoder while precomputing document representations like a bi-encoder?

blocks.title: Three ways to score a query against a document

scenes.caption: Bi-encoder: each side is squeezed into one vector, and the document side is computed offline. Cheap, but every detail of the document must survive in one vector.
Cross-encoder: query and document go through one transformer together. Every query token attends to every document token, but nothing can be cached, so cost grows with every candidate.
Late interaction (ColBERT): encode each side separately, but keep one vector per token. The only cross-talk is a cheap MaxSim step after encoding.
What happens at query time: one short encoder pass for the query, then MaxSim against stored document matrices. The document encoder never runs on the query path.

blocks.md: **Late interaction** means exactly that: the query and the document are encoded independently into *bags of contextual token vectors*, and their interaction is delayed until after encoding, where it is a cheap, parameter-free operation called **MaxSim** (lesson 2). Documents are encoded once at indexing time. The query is encoded once per query, not once per candidate.

blocks.prompt: ColBERT (BERT-base encoders, 128-dimensional token vectors) re-ranked the same BM25 top 1000. Guess its latency and quality next to the BERT-base cross-encoder's 10,700 ms and MRR@10 of 34.7.
blocks.reveal:
**61 ms and MRR@10 of 34.9** (ColBERT paper, Table 1), over 170x faster with about 7 billion FLOPs per query instead of 97 trillion.

The paper also trained a BERT-base cross-encoder with ColBERT's own loss, which reached 36.0, so late interaction does give up a little quality. Of the 61 ms, only 13 ms were query encoding plus MaxSim; the rest was gathering stored document vectors and copying them to the GPU.

blocks.title: MS MARCO dev MRR@10 when re-ranking BM25's top 1000

scenes.caption: Pre-BERT neural rerankers (3 to 28 ms each) lift MRR@10 from 16.7 to 29.0. Numbers from the ColBERT paper, Table 1.
BERT cross-encoders reach 34.7 to 36.5, at 10,700 ms (base) and 32,900 ms (large) per query.
ColBERT: 34.9 at 61 ms. Close to the cross-encoders, at the latency of the older neural models.

blocks.md: ColBERT is not a cross-encoder with a trick. Query tokens never attend to document tokens inside the transformer. All query-document interaction happens in MaxSim, which has no trainable parameters. That is exactly why document vectors can be stored in advance.
Late interaction = independent encoding (so documents are precomputed) + token-level matching at query time (so fine-grained evidence is not averaged away into one vector).

blocks.question: In a ColBERT system, which computation runs once per (query, candidate document) pair at search time?
options: The BERT pass over the document
The BERT pass over the query
The MaxSim between the query matrix and the document matrix
Projecting document tokens to 128 dimensions
blocks.explain: Document encoding (including the projection) happens offline, and the query is encoded once per query. Only the MaxSim, a few small matrix products and max operations, runs per candidate. A cross-encoder instead runs the whole transformer per pair.

blocks.question: The ColBERT paper reports that at re-ranking depth k = 10 the BERT-base cross-encoder needs about 180x more FLOPs than ColBERT, but at k = 1000 it needs 13,900x more. Why does the gap widen as k grows?
options: ColBERT skips most documents once k is large
The cross-encoder's cost grows with k (one transformer pass per document) while ColBERT's dominant cost, the single query encoding, does not
MaxSim becomes cheaper per document when k is large
BERT attention is quadratic in k
blocks.explain: The cross-encoder pays a full transformer pass over query plus document for each of the k candidates. ColBERT pays one query pass regardless of k, and the per-document MaxSim is tiny. Attention is quadratic in sequence length, not in k.

lessons.title: MaxSim: each query token finds its best document token

blocks.md: ColBERT normalizes every token vector to length 1, so a dot product is a cosine similarity between $-1$ and $1$. Given the query matrix $E_q$ (one row per query token) and the document matrix $E_d$ (one row per document token), the relevance score is:

blocks.caption: Equation 3 of the ColBERT paper. For each query vector, take its best similarity over all document vectors, then sum over query vectors.

blocks.md:
Let us run it on a toy. The query is *who founded pixar*. Real ColBERT vectors have 128 dimensions; ours have 4, and we hand-picked them so each axis has a meaning: Pixar-ness, founding, films and awards, and person.

- **Doc A**: *Pixar films won Oscars. It was started by Jobs.* We show 5 of its tokens: films, oscars, pixar, started, jobs.
- **Doc B**: *Pixar films won many Oscars.* Tokens: pixar, films, won, many, oscars.

Doc A answers the question. Doc B is on topic but does not. Note that neither document contains the word *founded*.

blocks.title: Doc A: cosine of every query token with every doc token

scenes.caption: Step 1: the 3 x 5 similarity matrix $E_q E_d^T$. Each cell is one dot product of 4-number unit vectors (simplified toy; real vectors have 128 numbers).
Step 2, row *who*: its best match is *jobs* at 0.91, because *jobs* sits near the person axis. Every other cell in the row is ignored.
Row *founded*: best match *started* at 0.98. A synonym match with zero word overlap, something BM25 cannot score.
Row *pixar*: best match *pixar* at 0.98. Exact matches still score high, since contextual vectors of the same word stay close.
Step 3: sum the row maxima. 0.91 + 0.98 + 0.98 = 2.87. That is the MaxSim score of Doc A.

blocks.prompt: Doc B contains *pixar* too, plus four film and award tokens. Before looking: will its *founded* row find a good match, and roughly what total do you expect?
blocks.reveal:
No good match exists for *founded*: its best cell is 0.32 (*won*). *who* is no better at 0.26. Only *pixar* matches well at 0.98. Total: **0.26 + 0.32 + 0.98 = 1.56**, far below Doc A's 2.87.

MaxSim rewards a document for covering *every* query token, which is how relevance usually works.

blocks.title: Doc B: same query, an on-topic document that does not answer

scenes.caption: Doc B's matrix. Its film and award tokens match nothing in this query, so most cells are dim.
Row maxima: *who* 0.26 (many), *founded* 0.32 (won), *pixar* 0.98 (pixar). Sum 1.56.
Doc A beats Doc B by 2.87 to 1.56. The gap comes almost entirely from *who* and *founded*, the tokens Doc B cannot match.

blocks.title: MaxSim is three lines of array code
blocks.code:
import numpy as np

def maxsim(Q, D):
    # Q: (Nq, dim), D: (Nd, dim), rows L2-normalized
    S = Q @ D.T            # cosine of every query/doc token pair
    best = S.max(axis=1)   # best doc token for each query token
    return best.sum()      # add the evidence over query tokens

score_A = maxsim(Q, D_A)

scenes.caption: Call with the toy query (3 x 4) and Doc A (5 x 4).
One matrix product gives all 15 cosines at once, the matrix from the first figure.
Max over the document axis: one number per query token.
Sum over query tokens.

blocks.md:
A few properties follow straight from the formula:

- Each query vector contributes at most 1, so the score lies between $-|E_q|$ and $|E_q|$.
- It sums over **query** tokens, not document tokens. Adding document tokens can only keep or raise each row's maximum; there is no length normalization.
- It has no trainable parameters, so all learning happens in the encoders.
- Each row is a nearest-neighbor question (which stored vector is closest to this query vector?), so vector indexes can find candidate documents without scoring every document. Lesson 5 uses this.

Why max and not average? The ColBERT ablation replaced max with average similarity and MRR@10 dropped noticeably. In the toy, the *founded* row of Doc A averages (0.03 + 0.02 + 0.18 + 0.98 + 0.49) / 5 = 0.34, even though the document contains a near-perfect match. Averaging punishes documents for having other content.

blocks.question: A query has 2 token vectors and a document has 3. The similarity matrix is [[0.2, 0.7, 0.4], [0.9, 0.1, 0.3]]. What is the MaxSim score?
blocks.explain: Row 1's best is 0.7 and row 2's best is 0.9, so 0.7 + 0.9 = 1.6. 2.6 sums every cell, 0.9 is the single largest cell, and 0.43 is the average.

blocks.question: You append 50 unrelated tokens (a cookie banner) to Doc A and re-encode. Ignoring small context shifts in the old tokens, what happens to its MaxSim score for this query?
options: It drops, because the score is normalized by document length
It stays the same or rises, because each row keeps its old maximum and can only find a higher one
It drops, because the extra tokens lower the average similarity
It doubles, because the matrix has more columns
blocks.explain: Each query row takes a max over document tokens. New columns can only tie or beat the old best match. This is why very long or noisy documents are usually split into passages before indexing.

lessons.title: Inside the encoders: markers, [MASK] padding and training

blocks.md:
ColBERT uses **one** BERT model for both sides and tells them apart with a marker token: `[Q]` for queries and `[D]` for documents, placed right after BERT's `[CLS]`. After BERT, a linear layer with no activation projects each 768-number output down to $m = 128$ numbers, and each vector is normalized to length 1.

The document side then drops the vectors of punctuation tokens, to store fewer vectors. The query side does something more surprising: it **pads the query with BERT's `[MASK]` token** up to a fixed length $N_q = 32$, and truncates longer queries.

blocks.title: Building the query input (toy Nq = 12; ColBERT uses 32)

scenes.caption: WordPiece tokenization of *who founded pixar* (simplified: the exact split depends on the vocabulary).
Add `[CLS]` and the query marker `[Q]` in front and `[SEP]` after, as the official tokenizer does.
Pad with `[MASK]` up to the fixed query length. These positions carry no words, but BERT still computes an output vector at each.
Every position becomes a 128-number unit vector, and all of them take part in MaxSim. The 5 mask vectors act as extra, learned query terms.

blocks.md: The paper calls this **query augmentation**: a soft, differentiable way for the model to *expand* the query with new terms or *re-weight* the terms that matter. Because the mask outputs are contextualized by the real query words, they learn to point toward related concepts. The ablation in the paper shows that removing it noticeably lowers MRR@10.

blocks.title: Adding one [MASK] vector to the toy query

scenes.caption: Doc A without the mask row: 2.87, as in lesson 2. (Simplified: we hand-picked a mask vector that leans toward *founding* and *Pixar*; real ones are learned.)
With the mask row, Doc A gains its best match *started* at 0.87. New score 2.87 + 0.87 = 3.74. In effect the founding concept now counts almost twice.
Doc B (same query): the mask row's best match is *pixar* at 0.54, so Doc B moves from 1.56 to 2.10.
The gap between the documents grew from 2.87 - 1.56 = 1.31 to 3.74 - 2.10 = 1.64. The mask re-weighted the query toward the part Doc B cannot answer.

blocks.md: **Training (ColBERT v1).** The data are triples: a query $q$, a relevant passage $d^+$ and a non-relevant passage $d^-$ (sampled from BM25 results). ColBERT scores both passages separately with MaxSim and applies a pairwise softmax cross-entropy loss. BERT is fine-tuned, while the linear layer and the `[Q]` and `[D]` embeddings are trained from scratch.

blocks.caption: Pairwise softmax cross-entropy: push the relevant passage's MaxSim score above the negative's.

blocks.md:
**Denoised supervision (ColBERTv2).** MS MARCO labels are sparse: many unlabeled passages are actually relevant, and BM25 negatives are easy. ColBERTv2 instead:

1. Indexes the training passages with an existing ColBERT model and retrieves the top-$k$ for each training query.
2. Scores those pairs with a 22M-parameter MiniLM **cross-encoder**.
3. Trains on 64-way tuples (query, one highly ranked or labeled passage, lower-ranked ones) with a KL-divergence loss that makes ColBERT's score distribution match the cross-encoder's, plus in-batch negatives.
4. Repeats this once to refresh the negatives.

On MS MARCO dev, MRR@10 went from 36.0 (ColBERT) to 39.7 (ColBERTv2).

This is the cross-encoder from the prerequisite course doing a new job: it is too slow to serve, but cheap enough to label a few million training pairs, and its knowledge is distilled into the fast late-interaction model.

blocks.question: A user types the 3-word query *who founded pixar*. With the default query length of 32, how many query vectors take part in MaxSim?
options: 3, one per word
4, one per WordPiece token
7, the tokens plus [CLS], [Q] and [SEP]
32, because the query is padded with [MASK] to 32 positions and every position yields a vector
blocks.explain: ColBERT pads every query to N_q = 32 with [MASK] tokens, and every position's output vector is used in MaxSim. So the query matrix is always 32 x 128, and the mask vectors act as learned expansion terms.

blocks.question: ColBERTv2 distills a cross-encoder with a KL-divergence loss over a 64-way score distribution instead of regressing the cross-encoder's raw scores with mean squared error. What is the reason the paper gives?
options: KL divergence is cheaper to compute than MSE
ColBERT's scores (sums of cosines) have a restricted scale that may not line up with the cross-encoder's output scale; KL compares the distributions over passages instead
MSE cannot be backpropagated through a max operation
The cross-encoder only outputs binary labels
blocks.explain: A sum of 32 cosines lives in a fixed range, while a cross-encoder's logits can be on any scale. Matching softmax distributions over the same 64 passages only asks ColBERT to rank them the same way, which is what retrieval needs.

lessons.title: Storage: why token vectors are heavy and how ColBERTv2 shrinks them

blocks.md: Late interaction stores one vector per document token. The raw size of a document's representation is simply:

blocks.caption: |E_d| = number of stored token vectors, m = dimensions per vector, b = bytes per number (4 for float32, 2 for float16).

blocks.prompt: Take a 100-token passage. A single-vector model stores one 768-number float32 vector. ColBERT stores 128-number float16 vectors, one per token. How many bytes each, and what is the ratio?
blocks.reveal:
Single vector: 768 x 4 = **3,072 bytes**.

ColBERT: 100 x 128 x 2 = **25,600 bytes**, about 8.3x larger, even though each token vector is 6x shorter than the single vector. Multiply by every passage in the corpus and late interaction becomes a storage problem first.

blocks.title: Bytes per document vs document length

scenes.caption: m = 128 (ColBERT's default). At 100 tokens: 25.6 KB in float16 versus 3.07 KB for one 768-d float32 vector. Storage grows linearly with length.
Shrinking m to 24 helps (4.8 KB at 100 tokens). ColBERT v1 found 24-d float16 vectors cost only about 1 point of MRR@10 on MS MARCO.
Back at m = 128, ColBERTv2's 2-bit residual encoding needs 36 bytes per token: 3.6 KB at 100 tokens, close to the single vector. The rest of this lesson builds it.

blocks.md: The ColBERT v1 paper measured the whole MS MARCO index (8.8M passages): 286 GiB at 128 dims in float32, 154 GiB in float16, 54 GiB at 48 dims, and 27 GiB at 24 dims (MRR@10 33.9 versus 34.9). Shrinking dimensions works, but there is a better trick.

**The observation behind ColBERTv2.** Token vectors cluster tightly by meaning. The authors ran k-means on about 600M MS MARCO token vectors and found that roughly 90% of clusters contain at most 16 distinct tokens (under 50% for random vectors), with clusters such as {photos, photo, pictures, photographs}. So a vector is well described by *which cluster it is in*, plus a small correction.

**Residual compression.** Store each vector $v$ as the id $t$ of its nearest centroid $C_t$ plus a coarsely quantized residual $\tilde r \approx v - C_t$, with each dimension of the residual stored in $b$ = 1 or 2 bits.

blocks.tex: \tilde v = C_t + \tilde r, \qquad \text{bits per vector} = \lceil \log_2 |C| \rceil + b \, n
blocks.caption: In practice n = 128 dims, 4 bytes hold the centroid id, and the residual takes 16 bytes (1-bit) or 32 bytes (2-bit): 20 or 36 bytes per vector, versus 256 bytes in float16.

blocks.md: How the official code picks the 2-bit buckets: on a held-out sample of token vectors, it computes all residuals and pools their values across every dimension. The 3 bucket **cutoffs** are the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles of those values, and each bucket's stored **value** is the 12.5th, 37.5th, 62.5th or 87.5th percentile, the middle of its bucket. Every dimension uses the same table. On decompression the code adds centroid and residual, then normalizes to length 1 again.

blocks.title: Compressing one toy 8-d vector with 2 bits per dimension

scenes.caption: A unit-length 8-d token vector (toy: 4 centroids and 400 sample vectors generated by our script; ColBERTv2 uses 128 dims and hundreds of thousands of centroids).
Find the nearest centroid (cosine 0.959). Storing only its id already gives a rough version of v.
The residual is what the centroid misses. Its entries are small, between -0.16 and 0.14.
Bucket each residual entry with cutoffs -0.071, 0.002 and 0.074 (the sample's quartiles). Bucket 0 to 3 fits in 2 bits: 16 bits for the whole residual.
Decoding replaces each 2-bit code (00, 10, 11, 01, 00, 01, 10, 11) with its bucket value: -0.125, -0.030, 0.035 or 0.123 (shown rounded).
Add to the centroid and re-normalize. Cosine with the original: 0.998, up from 0.959 for the centroid alone. With 1 bit per dimension it is 0.989.

blocks.md: How many centroids? The indexer uses $|C| = 2^{\lfloor \log_2(16\sqrt{n}) \rfloor}$ for $n$ token vectors, fitted with k-means on a sample. For about 600M vectors, $16\sqrt{6 \times 10^8} \approx 391{,}918$, which rounds down to $2^{18} = 262{,}144$ centroids.

scenes.caption: Vanilla ColBERT at 16-bit precision: 154 GiB for the 8.8M passages.
Residual compression: 25 GiB (2-bit) and 16 GiB (1-bit), including a 4.5 GiB inverted list. That is 6x to 10x smaller.
For scale: one 768-d float32 vector per passage is 8,841,823 x 3,072 bytes = 25.3 GiB, before any ANN index overhead.

blocks.md: Does compression hurt quality? Applied to a vanilla ColBERT model with MRR@10 of 36.2 on MS MARCO, 2-bit compression kept MRR@10 at 36.2 (Recall@50 82.1 to 82.3), and 1-bit gave 35.5. Summing many per-token maxima averages out small per-vector errors.
Compression is lossy per vector, and the 1-bit setting does cost measurable quality. Treat 2-bit as the safe default and verify 1-bit on your own evaluation set before shipping it.

blocks.question: A 200-token passage is stored with ColBERTv2 at 2 bits per dimension, 128 dimensions. How many bytes does it take, ignoring the inverted list?
options: 7,200 bytes
6,400 bytes
51,200 bytes
800 bytes
blocks.explain: Each vector is a 4-byte centroid id plus 128 x 2 bits = 32 bytes of residual, 36 bytes total. 200 x 36 = 7,200. 6,400 forgets the centroid id, 51,200 is float16 (200 x 128 x 2), and 800 counts only the ids.

blocks.question: Why does residual compression work so well on ColBERT vectors specifically?
options: ColBERT vectors are binary to begin with
MaxSim ignores all but the first few dimensions
Token vectors cluster tightly by word sense, so the residual from the nearest centroid is small and survives coarse quantization
The centroids are stored at 1 bit per dimension
blocks.explain: The paper's cluster analysis shows contextual token vectors concentrate near centroids that each hold a few related tokens. Small residuals lose little when cut to 2 or 1 bits per dimension. Random vectors do not cluster like this, so they would compress worse.

lessons.title: Searching millions of passages: candidates, centroids, PLAID

blocks.md:
So far we scored documents someone handed us. ColBERT can be used in two ways:

- **Re-ranking**: score the top 1000 from BM25 with MaxSim. Simple, but recall is capped by BM25.
- **End-to-end retrieval**: find candidates directly from the token vectors. ColBERT v1 put all document token vectors in a faiss IVFPQ index; each of the 32 query vectors fetched its 1000 nearest document vectors, those were mapped to their passages, and only those passages were scored with exact MaxSim. On MS MARCO this gave MRR@10 36.0 and Recall@1000 (share of relevant passages found in the top 1000) 96.8, versus 85.7 for a tuned BM25, at 458 ms per query.

ColBERTv2 replaced faiss with its own centroids: for each query vector, find the nearest `nprobe` centroids, use an inverted list (centroid to token vectors) to collect nearby vectors, decompress them, and keep the best candidates for exact scoring. The PLAID paper (Santhanam et al., 2022) measured that this vanilla pipeline spends most of its time on **index lookup and residual decompression**, often for 10k to 40k candidate passages.

PLAID's insight: the centroid ids are a fixed, discrete vocabulary. One matrix product scores every centroid against every query vector, and that matrix can be reused for every passage. A passage can then be scored approximately using **only its centroid ids**, replacing each token vector by its centroid, without touching any residual:

blocks.tex: S_{c,q} = C \, Q^{T}, \qquad \tilde S_{q,d} = \sum_{i=1}^{|Q|} \max_{t \in \text{cent}(d)} S_{c,q}[t, i]
blocks.caption: Centroid interaction: MaxSim where each document vector is replaced by its nearest centroid. cent(d) is the set of centroid ids of the passage's tokens.

blocks.title: Query vs centroid scores (toy: 3 query vectors, 6 centroids)

scenes.caption: One 3 x 6 product $Q C^T$ per query (the transpose of $S_{c,q}$ above). C0 is Pixar-like, C1 founding, C2 films and awards, C3 person, C4 and C5 unrelated. Toy numbers from our script.
Centroid pruning: a centroid's best score over all query vectors is 0.99, 0.99, 0.43, 0.97, 0.30, 0.15. With threshold $t_{cs}$ = 0.5, C2, C4 and C5 are dropped from every passage.
Doc A's tokens map to {C2, C2, C0, C1, C3}. After pruning: {C0, C1, C3}. Row maxima 0.97 + 0.99 + 0.99 = 2.95 approximate score.
Doc B maps to {C0, C2, C2, C2, C2}. Only C0 survives pruning: 0.10 + 0.19 + 0.99 = 1.28. Its four film tokens were never looked at.

blocks.prompt: Centroid scores are approximations of the true token scores. Do you expect the approximate ranking of 4 documents to match the exact MaxSim ranking exactly?
blocks.reveal:
Not exactly, and it does not need to. In our toy the approximate scores rank A, C, D, B while the exact scores rank A, B, C, D. The top document is the same, and the close calls in the middle are where the approximation errs.

That is why PLAID uses centroid scores only to **filter**, and runs exact MaxSim on the survivors. The PLAID paper measured that the top 10k passages by centroid-only scoring contain 99+% of vanilla ColBERTv2's top 1000.

blocks.title: Toy scores for 4 passages: approximate vs exact

scenes.caption: Centroid interaction without pruning: A 2.95, B 1.28, C 1.65, D 1.48.
With pruning ($t_{cs}$ = 0.5): D loses its C4 match and falls to 1.28. A is untouched, since its maxima came from strong centroids.
Exact MaxSim on decompressed vectors: A 2.87, B 1.56, C 1.54, D 1.52. Same winner; the order of the close runners-up changed.
Stage 1: score Q against all centroids once, take each query vector's nearest nprobe centroids, and collect every passage with a token in them (the inverted list maps centroid to passage ids).
Stage 2: approximate scores using only centroid ids, skipping centroids below $t_{cs}$. Keep the top ndocs passages.
Stage 3: re-score the survivors with all their centroids (no pruning). Keep ndocs/4.
Stage 4: only now load and decompress residuals, for a small set, and compute exact MaxSim. Return the top k.

blocks.md: The ColBERT repo picks defaults by `k`: for $k \le 10$, nprobe 1, $t_{cs}$ = 0.5, ndocs 256; for $k \le 100$, nprobe 2, $t_{cs}$ = 0.45, ndocs 1024; above that, nprobe 4, $t_{cs}$ = 0.4, ndocs $\max(4k, 4096)$. PLAID reports 2.5x to 7x lower latency than vanilla ColBERTv2 on a GPU and 9x to 45x on a CPU, with tens of milliseconds on a GPU even at 140M passages, while keeping retrieval quality.

Cheap approximate scores filter, exact scores decide. PLAID is the same funnel as BM25 followed by a cross-encoder, built inside one model: centroid ids are the cheap representation and decompressed vectors are the precise one.

blocks.question: What does PLAID's centroid pruning skip?
options: Query vectors whose norm is below the threshold
Passages shorter than ndocs tokens
The residuals of the final top k passages
Document tokens whose centroid scores below t_cs against every query vector, during the approximate stage
blocks.explain: Pruning drops centroids whose maximum score over all query vectors is below t_cs, so tokens assigned to them are ignored in stage 2. They come back in stage 3, and residuals are decompressed only in stage 4.

blocks.question: Why can PLAID compute the query-to-centroid score matrix once and reuse it for every candidate passage?
options: Because every passage stores a copy of the centroids
Because centroids are a fixed shared vocabulary: each passage token is just a centroid id, so its approximate score is a lookup into the same matrix
Because the query has only one vector
Because residuals are all zero after compression
blocks.explain: All passages draw their centroid ids from the same set C. Once C Q^T is computed, approximating any passage's MaxSim is a gather and max over rows of that matrix, with no new dot products and no decompression.

lessons.title: ColPali: late interaction over page images

blocks.md:
Retrieval over PDFs usually starts with an ingestion pipeline: a PDF parser or OCR to get text, a layout model to find titles, tables and figures, chunking, and sometimes a vision model to caption figures. The ColPali paper (Faysse et al., ICLR 2025) measured this on an NVIDIA L4: with OCR and captioning it took **7.22 s per page** to index, and charts, tables and layout still lose much of their meaning once flattened to text.

ColPali skips the pipeline and embeds the **page image** directly.

**Architecture.** ColPali starts from PaliGemma-3B, a vision-language model in which a SigLIP vision encoder cuts the image into patches and their embeddings are fed into the Gemma-2B language model alongside text tokens. ColPali keeps the language model's output vector at **every image patch** and projects each to 128 dimensions, as ColBERT does with tokens. A query is text, encoded by the same language model into one 128-d vector per token.

Because the language model maps patches into the same space as text, a query token like *revenue* can be compared directly with the patch showing a revenue chart. The score is plain MaxSim. The model card shows a page becoming **1030 vectors**; the paper explains them as 1024 patches (a 32 x 32 grid of 14-pixel patches over a 448 x 448 input) plus 6 tokens of the text prompt *Describe the image*.

blocks.title: Toy page, 6 x 6 patches: similarity of each patch to a query token

scenes.caption: Query token *revenue* against all 36 patches (toy: 5-d vectors, 36 patches instead of 1024). Left block is a revenue chart, right block a table, row 1 the title.
Its MaxSim is the single best patch: 0.899 on the patch where the revenue curve is drawn. Blank patches score near 0.
Query token *2023*: now the table header cell holding the year lights up, 0.922. The chart patch that won for *revenue* is dim.
Page score = 0.899 + 0.922 = 1.821. A prose-only page in our toy scores 0.356 + 0.236 = 0.592, since no patch strongly matches either token.

blocks.md: This also makes ColPali interpretable: for each query token you can overlay its patch similarities on the page and see which region it matched, as the paper's Figure 3 does.

scenes.caption: Text pipelines on ViDoRe, the paper's page-retrieval benchmark (10 tasks, English and French), scored by nDCG@5 (quality of the top 5, 100 is perfect): 65.5 and 67.0.
Single-vector image models: SigLIP 51.4, fine-tuned 58.6. Feeding patches through the language model and averaging them into one vector (BiPali): 58.8.
Same model as BiPali, but keeping one vector per patch and scoring with MaxSim: 81.3. Late interaction is the step that beats the text pipelines.

blocks.prompt: Estimate ColPali's raw storage per page: 1030 vectors of 128 dimensions in float16. How does it compare with the paper's 8.60 KB per page for BGE-M3 dense vectors?
blocks.reveal:
1030 x 128 x 2 = **263,680 bytes = 257.5 KiB** per page, the figure the paper reports. That is about 30x the BGE-M3 size.

For 1M pages: 263.68 GB raw. This is the same storage problem as lesson 4, at roughly 10x more vectors per item.

blocks.md:
The mitigations are the ones you already know:

- **Binarization**: Vespa's ColBERT embedder can store each token vector as 1 bit per value, `tensor<int8>(token{}, x[16])` for 128 dims, which it describes as 32x smaller than float. A ColPali page would drop to 1030 x 16 = 16,480 bytes.
- **Token pooling**: averaging similar patch vectors. The ColPali paper reports that a pool factor of 3 removes 66.7% of vectors while keeping 97.8% of performance, though text-dense pages degrade more.
- **Two-stage search**: Vespa's docs position ColBERT tensors for *ranking*, with candidates retrieved by a document-level vector or lexical match first.

At query time the paper reports about 30 ms to encode a query, and roughly 1 ms per 1000 pages for brute-force MaxSim.

        distance=models.Distance.COSINE,

blocks.md: Late interaction is not free accuracy. You pay in index size, in memory bandwidth at query time, and in engine support. For large text corpora a common design is a cheap first stage (BM25 or a single-vector index) with ColBERT or ColPali scoring a few hundred candidates.
ColBERT and ColPali are the same idea at different granularities: keep one vector per token or patch, precompute the document side, and let each query token pick its best match.

blocks.question: BiPali and ColPali use the same PaliGemma backbone and training data, yet score 58.8 and 81.3 on ViDoRe. What is the difference between them?
options: ColPali runs OCR on the page first
BiPali averages the patch vectors into one vector per page; ColPali keeps one vector per patch and scores with MaxSim
ColPali uses a larger language model
BiPali only sees the page title
blocks.explain: The paper builds the model step by step. BiPali mean-pools the language model's patch outputs into a single dense vector. ColPali keeps every patch vector and uses late interaction, which is the 22.5-point jump.

blocks.question: You index 1 million PDF pages with ColPali at float16 and 1030 vectors per page. Roughly how much raw vector storage do you need?
options: About 264 MB
About 2.6 GB
About 264 GB
About 2.6 TB
blocks.explain: 263,680 bytes per page x 1,000,000 pages = 263.68 GB. This is why binarization (about 16.5 GB here) or pooling matters at scale.

blocks.question: Which corpus is the strongest fit for ColPali over an OCR plus text-embedding pipeline?
options: 50,000 pages of financial reports full of charts and tables, where indexing speed matters
100 million short plain-text chat messages
A code search index over source files
A product catalog searched only by exact SKU
blocks.explain: ColPali's gains are largest on visually rich pages (infographics, figures, tables) and it skips slow OCR and captioning. Plain text at huge scale gains little from page images and pays heavily in storage; exact-match lookups need no neural retriever.
